narrative:
The 2024 Washington Nationals entered the season as a team still in the process of rebuilding, and the opening days set an uncomfortable tone. Hunter Harvey and Kyle Finnegan, the arms entrusted with late-inning situations, were immediately exposed in the first two games — surrendering doubles, home runs, and momentum before March was even over. The bullpen's vulnerability would become the season's defining wound, one that never fully healed.

April offered some hope, with a dead-even 13-13 mark suggesting the Nationals could compete. May brought genuine excitement in flashes — CJ Abrams emerging as a legitimate offensive force with a three-run homer that was among the season's most electrifying moments, and Luis García Jr. delivering clutch blasts. But for every spark, the bullpen found a way to douse it, and the team limped to a losing record in May. June stayed close to .500, with Jesse Winker providing some punch, but a catastrophic Hunter Harvey outing in San Diego — surrendering a three-run single that swung nearly three-quarters of a win in a single pitch — symbolized how fragile the team's margins really were.

July and August were when the bottom fell out in the standings. Kyle Finnegan's nightmare season reached its nadir on July 29th, when a Corbin Carroll two-run homer — the single most damaging play of the Nationals' year — encapsulated a bullpen that simply could not hold leads. The arrival of James Wood provided a genuine bright spot and a reason for optimism, his raw power flashing in a multi-run home run in late July. But the team went 10-16 in July and 12-15 in August, any wins coming in spite of rather than because of the relief corps.

September offered little redemption in the win column — a 10-16 finish sealed a 71-91 record — but the month did produce the season's most heartening individual moments. Ildemaro Vargas delivered a clutch go-ahead double against Pittsburgh, and Joey Gallo connected for a three-run shot that gave the home crowd something to cheer. For a franchise still waiting for its next competitive window, these glimpses from young players like Wood, Abrams, and García were the real story of 2024: not the losses, but the foundation quietly being laid beneath them.

chapters.title: Bullpen Blues from Day One
chapters.description: Washington's relievers are torched in the opening series, foreshadowing the season's central flaw before April even begins.

chapters.title: Abrams and García Ignite Hope
chapters.description: CJ Abrams and Luis García Jr. emerge as genuine offensive weapons, giving the Nationals a competitive pulse through May.

chapters.title: Holding On Through June
chapters.description: The team stays near .500 but Harvey's meltdown in San Diego signals the limits of a roster that can't absorb late-inning collapses.

chapters.title: July Unravels
chapters.description: A catastrophic Finnegan implosion against Arizona in late July becomes the low point of a brutal month that drops Washington deep into the cellar.

chapters.title: Wood Arrives, Losses Mount
chapters.description: James Wood's debut power flash offers a glimpse of the future even as the team trudges through another losing August.

chapters.title: September Sparks in a Lost Season
chapters.description: Vargas, Gallo, and the young core produce bright moments down the stretch, hinting at what the Nationals might eventually become.
